questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating the Product of a Constant and the Exponential Function, Plus a Constant
questions.worked_solution:
The derivative of ${e}^{x}$ is just ${e}^{x}$ itself. On the other hand, $ln⁡8$ is a constant, so its derivative is $0.$

Using the addition rule, then, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{e}^{x}+ln⁡8) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{e}^{x})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ln⁡8) \\  & =6\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x})+0 \\  & =6{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x)=9{e}^{x}+ln⁡4$, the slope of the tangent line at $x=ln⁡2$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The derivative of ${e}^{x}$ is just ${e}^{x}$ itself. On the other hand, $ln⁡4$ is a constant, so its derivative is $0.$

First, using the addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(9{e}^{x}+ln⁡4) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(9{e}^{x})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ln⁡4) \\  & =9\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x})+0 \\  & =9{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=ln⁡2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=ln⁡2} & ={(9{e}^{x})\,|}_{x=ln⁡2} \\  & =9{e}^{ln⁡2} \\  & =9\cdot 2 \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x)=5{e}^{x}+1$, find the slope of the tangent at $x=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
The derivative of ${e}^{x}$ is just ${e}^{x}$ itself. On the other hand, $1$ is a constant, so its derivative is $0.$

First, using the addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5{e}^{x}+1) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5{e}^{x})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\  & =5\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x})+0 \\  & =5{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & ={(5{e}^{x})\,|}_{x=0} \\  & =5{e}^{0} \\  & =5\cdot 1 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The derivative of ${e}^{x}$ is just ${e}^{x}$ itself. On the other hand, $-ln⁡11$ is a constant, so its derivative is $0.$

First, using the addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{e}^{x}-ln⁡11) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{e}^{x})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-ln⁡11) \\  & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x})+0 \\  & =2{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x)={x}^{2}+2x+6{e}^{x}$, find the slope of the tangent at $x=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, using the addition and the power rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+2x+6{e}^{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{e}^{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)+6\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x}) \\  & =2x+2+6{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & ={(2x+2+6{e}^{x})\,|}_{x=0} \\  & =2\cdot 0+2+6\cdot {e}^{0} \\  & =2+6\cdot 1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x)=2{e}^{x}-3{x}^{2}$, find the slope of the tangent at $x=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, using the addition and the power rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{e}^{x}-3{x}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{e}^{x})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2}) \\  & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x})-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\  & =2{e}^{x}-3(2x) \\  & =2{e}^{x}-6x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & ={(2{e}^{x}-6x)\,|}_{x=0} \\  & =2{e}^{0}-6\cdot 0 \\  & =2\cdot 1-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x)=6{x}^{7}+2{e}^{x}$, the exact value of the slope of the tangent line at $x=-1$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, using the addition and the power rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{x}^{7}+2{e}^{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{x}^{7})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{e}^{x}) \\  & =6\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{7})+2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x}) \\  & =6(7{x}^{6})+2{e}^{x} \\  & =42{x}^{6}+2{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=-1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=-1} & ={(42{x}^{6}+2{e}^{x})\,|}_{x=-1} \\  & =42(-1)^{6}+2{e}^{-1} \\  & =42\cdot 1+\frac{2}{e} \\  & =42+\frac{2}{e}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x)=2{e}^{x}+4{x}^{2}-3$, find the slope of the tangent at $x=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, using the addition and the power rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{e}^{x}+4{x}^{2}-3) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{e}^{x})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-3) \\  & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x})+4\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+0 \\  & =2{e}^{x}+8x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(2{e}^{x}+8x)\,|}_{x=1} \\  & =2\cdot {e}^{1}+8\cdot 1 \\  & =2e+8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x)=11{e}^{x}+8{x}^{2}-12x-20$, find the slope of the tangent at $x=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the addition and the power rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(11{e}^{x}+8{x}^{2}-12x-20) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(11{e}^{x})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8{x}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(12x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(20) \\  & =11\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x})+8\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})-12\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(20) \\  & =11{e}^{x}+8(2x)-12(1)-0 \\  & =11{e}^{x}+16x-12.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=0$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & ={(11{e}^{x}+16x-12)|}_{x=0} \\  & =11{e}^{0}+16\cdot 0-12 \\  & =11\cdot 1+0-12 \\  & =11-12 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating an Exponential Function with a Base Other Than e
questions.problem: Given that $f(x)={3}^{x}+5{e}^{x}$, find the instantaneous rate of change at $x=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({3}^{x}+5{e}^{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({3}^{x})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}(5{e}^{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({3}^{x})+5\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x}) \\  & ={3}^{x}ln⁡3+5{e}^{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change at $x=0$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & ={({3}^{x}ln⁡3+5{e}^{x})|}_{x=0} \\  & ={3}^{0}ln⁡3+5{e}^{0} \\  & =1\cdot ln⁡3+5\cdot 1 \\  & =ln⁡3+5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x)={5}^{x}-6{x}^{3}+4x-1$, the slope of the tangent at $x=0$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({5}^{x}-6{x}^{3}+4x-1) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({5}^{x})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{x}^{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({5}^{x})-6\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})+4\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\  & =ln⁡(5)\cdot {5}^{x}-6(3{x}^{2})+4(1)-0 \\  & =ln⁡(5)\cdot {5}^{x}-18{x}^{2}+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=0$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & ={(ln⁡(5)\cdot {5}^{x}-18{x}^{2}+4)|}_{x=0} \\  & =ln⁡(5)\cdot {5}^{0}-18(0)^{2}+4 \\  & =ln⁡(5)\cdot 1-0+4 \\  & =ln⁡(5)+4.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Differentiating the Product of a Constant and the Exponential Function, Plus a Constant
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The derivative of $e^x$ is just $e^x$ itself. On the other hand, $\ln 3$ is a constant, so its derivative is $0.$

Using the addition rule, then, we have 

$$
\eqalign{
f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(3e^x + \ln 3\right)\
                                                  &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left( 3e^x\right) +  \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left( \ln 3 \right)\
                                                  &= 3\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(e^x\right) + 0\
                                                  &= 3 e^x.
}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Differentiating the Product of a Constant and the Exponential Function, Plus a Polynomial
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the addition and the power rules, we get

$$
\eqalign{ 
                          f'(x)             &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(4e^x+3x^{4} - x^2 \right)\
                                             &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(4e^x\right)+\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(3x^{4}\right) -\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(x^{2}\right) \
					     &= 4\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(e^x\right)+3\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(x^{4}\right) - 2x \			
                                             &=  4 e^x+  3 \cdot 4x^{3} - 2x \
                                             &=  4 e^x+  12x^{3} - 2x.
}
$$
